title: Giri Beats Abdusattorov As Bayegan Pendik Wins European Club Cup
summary: GM Anish Giri scored a crushing win over GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov as top-seed Bayegan Pendik Chess Sports Club beat defending champion SuperChess Romania 3.5-2.5 to win the 2026 European Chess Club Cup. Novy Bor Chess Club missed out on gold on tiebreaks despite overpowering Elektroprivreda 4.5-1.5, while GM Boris Gelfand-led Rishon LeZion A snatched bronze by winning the battle of the underdogs against Cheddleton Savills Catering 5.5-0.5. Defending champion Cercle d'Echecs de Monte-Carlo clinched the 2026 European Women's Chess Club Cup after a 4-0 win in the final round helped them finish above CE Gambit Bonnevoie on tiebreaks, with Monte-Carlo also claiming individual gold on boards one (GM Aleksandra Goryachkina), two (GM Koneru Humpy), and four (GM Elisabeth Paehtz). Sirmium Sremska Mitrovica took bronze after a 3.5-0.5 victory over the round-six heroes, Odlar Yurdu. Meanwhile, 11-year-old FM Bodhana Sivanandan won on demand to score her final IM norm and become the seventh youngest IM of all time—a feat we've covered in this separate report. Bayegan Pendik Chess Sports Club surprisingly easily won the battle of the leaders against SuperChess Romania, but looked on nervously as Novy Bor Chess Club racked up a big score to beat Elektroprivreda—the margin of the win could matter for tiebreaks. In the end, however, Bayegan Pendik took gold by 8.5 tiebreak points. Rishon LeZion A, who won all their matches except for a loss to Novy Bor in round four, took bronze, while SuperChess Romania still earned a spot in the 2027 European Chess Super League. title: Nakamura Wins With 'GOAT Horns'; Caruana, Maghsoodloo Repeat In 3 0 Thursday
summary: GM Hikaru Nakamura played the GOAT Horns Variation, referencing a recent advertisement featuring soccer star Lionel Messi, on his way to winning the first 3 0 Thursday tournament on October 22. GMs Fabiano Caruana and Parham Maghsoodloo won the second and third events, respectively. For both of them, it was a repeat of their tournament victories the prior week. Inspired by Messi's recent advertisement, Nakamura played the GOAT Horns Variation (1...a6 and 2...c6) in each of his black games throughout the first tournament. The offbeat opening served Nakamura well, as he scored 4.5/5 with the black pieces. He often recovered from somewhat dubious positions, like this critical 10th-round win against GM Oleksandr Bortnyk.

title: Niemann Wins Freestyle Friday, Preventing Movahed Repeat
summary: GM Hans Niemann won his third Freestyle Friday on October 23, scoring nine points and defeating last week's winner, GM Sina Movahed, on tiebreaks, as well as in their individual encounter in round 10. Like Movahed, the win was Niemann's first in the Freestyle Friday Championship (FFC) era of the tournament. With the win he climbed into the top 10 in the FFC standings. IM Sagar Shah streamed and commentated for Freestyle Chess: Niemann made one draw, and Movahed two, in the first four rounds, and Niemann then also lost his first game out of the first break to eventual fourth-place finisher IM Reza Mahdavi. In an attempt to get tricky, Niemann missed Mahdavi's own counter-trick, and had to resign only a few moves later.

title: Bodhana, 11, Breaks Judit Polgar’s Record To Become Youngest Female IM In History
summary: The extraordinary FM Bodhana Sivanandan has done it again. On Friday, the 11-year-old prodigy achieved yet another record, becoming the youngest girl ever to complete the requirements for the International Master title, securing her third and final norm at the European Club Cup in Budva, Montenegro. Bodhana defeated WIM Viktoria Johansson of Sweden's Wasa SK in the seventh and final round, finishing on 5.5/7 on board one for her team, She Plays To Win Lionesses A. With a rating performance of 2465, she achieved her third and final IM norm. At 11 years, seven months, and 16 days, that means she has broken a female age record held by GM Judit Polgar since 1988. The Hungarian earned the IM title at 12, before going on to become the strongest female player in chess history. Congratulations to 11-year-old IM Bodhana Sivanandan on scoring her final IM norm to become the 7th youngest IM in chess history — and the youngest female IM ever! https://t.co/odYTIrc3Qn https://t.co/gqWP8GkCcg In a post-game interview with WCM Tallulah Roberts on the official broadcast, Bodhana, when asked about the achievement, said she was already looking toward her next goal. "I'm happy about that but hopefully I'm able to get grandmaster soon as well!" she said. I'm happy about that but hopefully I'm able to get grandmaster soon as well!—Bodhana Sivanandan The British prodigy from Harrow outside London has not only broken a record Polgar held for 38 years, but she is also the seventh-youngest player of all time to qualify for the title, according to Chess.com's research. She is exactly one month older than World Championship Challenger GM Javokhir Sindarov was when he achieved his IM title in 2017, while the reigning champion GM Gukesh Dommaraju was almost two months older in 2018. She is one of only ten players to complete the title before turning 12. "You can only describe her as a generational talent, I am delighted that it's happening," IM Malcolm Pein, Director of International Chess and External Relations at the English Chess Federation, told Chess.com. "I think we stopped being surprised by her achievements in the last year." The achievement comes less than a month after she became the youngest player ever to fulfill the requirements for the Woman Grandmaster (WGM) title at the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. While still awaiting formal approval for that title, she has now passed the required 2400 live rating during the European Club Cup, and also completed the requirements for the higher, open IM title, which is available to players of any gender. Playing on board one for She Plays To Win Lionesses A, Sivanandan recovered from an opening-round defeat against former Women's World Championship challenger GM Aleksandra Goryachkina. She struck back with two wins, including this one over IM Olga Badelka.

title: Magnus Carlsen Headlines New Barcelona Rapid Event With 1-Second Increment
summary: GM Magnus Carlsen wants more events that are exciting to watch. Now he has helped shape one. The world number-one will headline the inaugural MOVE Cup in Barcelona on January 19–20, 2027, an eight-player rapid tournament with €300,000 in prizes and a one-second increment intended to keep the pressure on. The two-day event is backed by sportsbook technology supplier BETBY, which has sponsored Carlsen since 2024. A charity hand-and-brain event on January 18 will precede the main competition, which takes place alongside ICE Barcelona, a trade show for the gaming industry. Organizers said the tournament is guaranteed to take place in Barcelona for the next three years. Carlsen is the only confirmed participant, but the remaining seven grandmasters, expected to be some of the top names in the world, will be announced in the coming weeks. “The fact that Magnus Carlsen is involved speaks for itself," eight-time Spanish chess champion GM Miguel Illescas said at a press conference in Barcelona on October 20. Carlsen noted how chess has grown in recent years, but argued he wants events that can attract more fans. "I think we kind of lack events that bring chess to an audience that can have a better spectator experience that makes it more exciting," he said. We lack events that bring chess to an audience that can have a better spectator experience that makes it more exciting.—Magnus Carlsen At the MOVE Cup, spectators on site will be able to follow live commentary through headphones, with scores displayed on large screens, similar to Chess.com's Speed Chess Championship Finals and the Esports World Cup Final. Magnus Carlsen discussing the format of the Move Cup during yesterday’s press conference. https://t.co/jhXT4EkHe1 "This will be a lot of fun and really exciting to follow," Carlsen said. The world number-one has played a part in designing the tournament format. Games will be played with 10 minutes plus a one-second increment. "One second is just about enough to physically make the moves," he explained. “Two seconds, the problem is that you can accumulate time," he said, suggesting a 1.5-second increment would be ideal. One second is just about enough to physically make the moves. Two seconds, the problem is that you can accumulate time.—Magnus Carlsen The first day consists of a round-robin with the eight players, with the top four players advancing to semifinals. The knockout phase will be played as best of three games, while the final will be best of five games. The launch also introduces the MOVE Foundation, which will receive a €300,000 contribution matching the players’ prize fund. Organizers say any additional money raised during the tournament will be divided equally between the prize fund and the foundation. The foundation’s stated priorities include chess development, support for young talent, and research into chess and mental health. Board member Inese Dabola said it would work with existing projects as well as develop its own programs, with information about donations and activities published online. "We believe chess has a lot to offer today," Dabola said. It's worth noting that the MOVE Cup overlaps with Tata Steel Chess, a tournament that has been on the chess calendar for decades. In 2027, it runs from January 15-31 in Wijk aan Zee, the Netherlands. Carlsen has won the Dutch tournament eight times, but has not played there since 2023. Asked by Chess.com about the clash, he smiled: "It means that I’m not playing next year," adding that he has a great relationship with the Dutch organizers. "On a more general point, it would of course be good if there was more coordination in the chess world and that it were less fragmented. But it is what it is." For Carlsen, the MOVE Cup marks yet another speed chess tournament on his calendar. A highlight of the press conference was Illescas, who worked with former World Champion GM Vladimir Kramnik, asking whether Carlsen would consider returning to the World Championship cycle for $20 million. "Most people have a price, obviously," Carlsen said. "But I am not going to speculate what that price is. From a sporting perspective, there are a lot of things in chess that interest me more than a classical match." title: 2026 U.S. Championship: Wesley So and Rachael Li claim titles
summary: GM Wesley So and WIM Rachael Li are the new U.S. chess champions. So captured his fourth American chess crown, while Li became the youngest player to win the title on her debut. The 2026 U.S. Chess Championship and the 2026 U.S. Women’s Chess Championship were 12-player, single round-robin tournaments with classical time controls, held from October 9 to 22 in Saint Louis. The Saint Louis Chess Club has long been the driving force behind the U.S. Chess Championships, hosting the nation’s most prestigious chess events and showcasing the country’s top talent. The 2026 edition brought everything under one roof, uniting U.S. Chess with the Saint Louis Chess Club to create a seamless experience for players, fans, and the broader chess community. The Open event featured a $250,000 prize fund, including $55,000 for first place, while the Women’s event offered $152,000, with $35,000 for first. In the Open event, top seeds and rating favorites defending champion Fabiano Caruana and So got off to a strong start, sharing the lead after Round 4 with 3/4 points. In Round 5, Caruana suffered a defeat at the hands of Andy Woodward but struck back in the next round to catch up with So. However, after So made a decisive push in Rounds 7 and 8, defeating Ray Robson and Woodward, the fate of the title appeared sealed. Heading into the final round a full point ahead of Caruana and Grigory Oparin, So needed only a draw against Sam Sevian to win outright, but his opponent had a different agenda. After Caruana did his part, defeating Awonder Liang with a crushing attack, and Oparin drew with Robson, all eyes were on the Sevian–So game, in which Sevian (White) emerged with an extra pawn in a rook endgame. So put up a stubborn defense and had a chance to escape with a draw on move 48, but he missed this opportunity and ended up in a lost position. The rest was smooth sailing for Sevian, who scored a full point, inflicting the only defeat on So in the tournament. With this result, Caruana and So tied for first place with 7/11 points each. To determine the champion, a tiebreak consisting of two rapid games and two blitz games (if necessary) was played the following day. In the first topsy-turvy rapid game, So, playing with the black pieces, had every chance but let his advantage slip away, and the game ended in a draw. With the colors reversed, So grabbed the initiative early on and converted his advantage convincingly to secure the title. The Women’s event turned into an exciting race between Alice Lee and Rachael Li. Lee started right out of the gate with four straight victories in Rounds 2–5 and appeared to be on her way to the title. However, Li defeated Lee with the black pieces in a Queen’s Indian Defense, catching up to her in the standings. Their paths diverged in Round 9 when Lee suffered another defeat at the hands of Irina Krush, while Li ground down Nazi Paikidze in a drawish knight endgame. Going into the final round a full point ahead of her main competitor, Li secured a comfortable draw in her game against Anna Zatonskih to clinch the title. Lee won her final-round game against Anna Sargsyan and finished a half-point behind the champion, while Krush took third place to complete the podium. Photos: Saint Louis Chess Club / Crystal Fuller and Lennart Ootes

title: FIDE extends fee waiver for Rapid and Blitz through 2027
summary: The FIDE Council has announced the extension of its rating fee waiver for all Rapid and Blitz tournaments through 2027. The FIDE Council stated that the decision aims to expand player participation and promote chess. These rating fees, covered by federations, are outlined in the Financial Regulations of the FIDE Handbook. According to the regulations, “All rated tournaments are subject to rating fees. The FIDE Council, at its sole discretion, may waive or reduce rating fees for Rapid and Blitz tournaments for a given year.” The fee waiver was first introduced for the 2021–2024 period. Since then, the total waived fees have approached €2 million. While rating fees are a source of revenue for FIDE, this waiver is widely welcomed by national federations, as it supports both organizers and players. This initiative eases financial pressures on organizers and federations while encouraging more Rapid and Blitz events. Such support is crucial for the growth of chess, especially in regions with limited resources. The decision has been added to the FIDE Handbook and takes effect immediately.

title: Review: My favourite FritzTrainer courses
summary:
For Jochen Schwarz, club player from Bremen, FritzTrainer courses have become an essential part of his hobby. Over the past ten years, he has studied numerous courses and now shares some of the favourites that have impressed him most.

When I returned to competitive chess in 2016 after a lengthy break, ChessBase FritzTrainer courses became my preferred source of information for brushing up on my chess knowledge. I enjoy the combination of videos, databases and interactive exercises, and FritzTrainer courses soon became something of a "hobby within a hobby". Of the more than 100 FritzTrainer courses I have watched or worked through over the past ten years, certain courses and authors have proved particularly instructive. I would like to introduce a selection of them here.

Opening Courses

What these courses have in common is that they provide the foundations for building a reliable opening repertoire. The emphasis is on understanding the tactical and strategic characteristics of the openings and variations, rather than simply compiling lines. Of course, such courses tend to "age" relatively quickly, as opening theory develops at a rapid pace. Nevertheless, they retain their value over time because the essential characteristics of the openings do not change.

As ChessBase customers, we have plenty of opportunities to expand the repertoires we have developed with the help of these courses and keep them up to date using other products, such as the Opening Encyclopaedia:

... the Fritz Powerbook:

... or the opening articles in ChessBase Magazine:

These resources allow us to continually expand and update our repertoires.

PowerPlay 23-25 by Daniel King

PowerPlay volumes 23–25 provide a complete and solid repertoire for Black against 1.d4 (as well as 1.c4 and 1.Nf3), based on the moves ...d5, ...e6 and ...Nf6. I consider the didactic quality and the careful selection of variations and recommendations in these courses to be simply "outstanding". Volume 23 covers the Queen's Gambit Declined, Volume 24 the Catalan, and Volume 25 Queen's Pawn Openings without c4.

I recently published a detailed review of Daniel King's PowerPlay series .

A Repertoire against the Sicilian, ABC of the English Opening und Queen's Gambit Declined von Lorin D'Costa

For me, the courses by IM Lorin D'Costa (some of them together with Nick Murphy, who asks the master typical questions from an amateur's perspective) are something of a "hidden gem" for players who are unfamiliar with these openings but would like to learn them. The focus is on getting started and understanding the fundamental ideas, which are explained very clearly and instructively through illustrative games and exercises.

A Classical Guide to the French Defence and Anti-London System

by Yannick Pelletier

Another author who is particularly good at explaining complex theory to beginners is Swiss GM Yannick Pelletier. I have already discussed his " Classical Guide to the French " in my review of courses on the French Defence . In my view, this course, together with Daniel King's PowerPlay 22 , provides an ideal introduction for anyone wishing to take up this opening.

Pelletier's " Anti-London System " course has a different background. A few years ago, there was a real craze for the London System ( 1.d4 followed by 2.Bf4 or 3.Bf4 ), and it sometimes seemed as though White could obtain an advantage almost effortlessly with this setup. Since then, the enthusiasm has subsided somewhat, and the London System is now regarded as one of many good options for White.

With his course, Pelletier wanted to demonstrate that Black has several good ways of meeting the London System, depending on which opening Black normally plays against 1.d4 and 2.c4: systems based on ...d5 or ...g6, the Queen's Indian Defence, the Queen's Gambit, the Benoni, the Benko Gambit or the Dutch Defence.

Courses on Tactics and Strategy

Calculation Training and Extreme Calculation Training by Robert Ris

I have already discussed Robert Ris's excellent "Calculation Training" series in an earlier review .

The first two volumes, " Calculation Training " and " Extreme Calculation Training ", remain my favourites. For me, the combination of thoroughly annotated examples and interactive exercises, which are also explained in great detail, makes these courses some of the highlights among FritzTrainer releases focusing on tactics and calculation.

The products were provided to the author by ChessBase for review.

title: Wesley So beats Fabiano Caruana in tiebreaks, wins fourth US Chess Championship title
summary:
In the end, Wesley So did it! Following his bitter defeat to Sam Sevian in the final round of the 2026 US Championship - which ended his 48-game unbeaten run at the event - he defeated Fabiano Caruana 1½–½ in the rapid playoff for the title. It was a thrilling encounter, not without mistakes, but full of interesting moments. | Photo: Lennart Ootes / Saint Louis Chess Club

"This title is so hard to get"

The first exciting moment came as early as move 11 of the first game: in a variation of the Nimzo-Indian, Wesley So surprised with the novelty 11...Nb6!? , a move that at first glance looked like a mistake and invited White to win a piece. But Fabiano Caruana apparently considered the gift poisoned and opted for a quiet continuation.

So continued to play energetically and strongly, however, and gradually increased his advantage - on move 27 he won a pawn, and on move 34 he missed a forced win. But then the game turned around, and Caruana generated more and more counterplay in a tactically complicated position in which both sides had only seconds left on the clock. After 72 moves, the game ended drawn by repetition.

The opening in the second game was also surprising. This time around, it was Caruana who came up with the surprise. Playing black, he chose a dubious, speculative gambit line. So responded cautiously and returned the pawn, but in doing so, secured a clear advantage.

Then, once again, the tension of the playoff and the long tournament began to show: Caruana miscalculated and blundered a piece. A few moves later he resigned, and Wesley So was declared the 2026 US chess champion!

In his interview with Maurice Ashley after the playoff, Caruana tried to explain why he had chosen the double-edged opening. "I knew this line existed. I don't know why I chose it. I mean, it's probably a bit too risky".

He was also puzzled by his tactical oversight at the critical moment of the game: "I thought that his queen had to go to a4. I didn't really spend any time calculating, I just went for it, which was obviously insane".

More generally, Caruana was frustrated with his rapid-chess form. "I have lost about 110 Elo points in a year. But I don't know what's been going on. I haven't been able to find my form".

Wesley So, who despite all the excitement on the board appeared calm, focused and composed throughout the playoff, revealed in his interview after the round how much the defeat against Sevian had affected him. "I think I only slept for two or three hours, and I was not in the mood to play today at all".

But he praised his opponent: "Sam had a very tough tournament. I was shocked with the way he played - it was a very good game. But I also played very badly".

Despite winning the title, So was not satisfied with his play overall: "I don't think I deserved to win this year, but I'll take it of course." He added that both players had made many mistakes in the playoff, noting that both contenders were very tired.

For all his self-criticism, So was ultimately satisfied: "I am very happy to have won my fourth US Championship. This title is very difficult to win, especially now that so many strong grandmasters are taking part".

Check out Karsten Müller's Endgame Magic show with Wesley So!

Yet another big tournament coming up

After a short break, chess continues in Saint Louis: from 27 to 29 October, the tournament Clutch Chess: Champions Showdown will take place. Fabiano Caruana, Hikaru Nakamura, Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu and Javokhir Sindarov will be competing.

The four grandmasters will play an 18-game rapid tournament in which wins become increasingly valuable as the event progresses. Six games will be played on each of the three days. On the first day, a win is worth one point, on the second day two points and on the third day three points. A total prize fund of US$425,000 is at stake, including additional bonuses for games won and a jackpot for the tournament winner.
